title: Introduction
focus: the origin of the novel and the idea of creation

teacherSummary.text: Writing in 1831, Shelley explains how the novel began: a rainy summer near Geneva in 1816, a ghost-story contest with Byron and Percy Shelley, conversations about galvanism, and a waking vision of a 'pale student of unhallowed arts' kneeling beside the thing he had put together. She calls the book her 'hideous progeny.'

vocabulary.definition: The quality or state of being flat, thin, or insipid
vocabulary.context: The illustrious poets also, annoyed by the platitude of prose, speedily relinquished their uncongenial task.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “platitude”: -ude (Latin -udo, "state of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The act or form of calling for the assistance or presence of some superior being
vocabulary.context: I felt that blank incapability of invention which is the greatest misery of authorship, when dull Nothing replies to our anxious invocations.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “invocation”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in") + voc (Latin vocare, "to call") + -ation (Latin -atio, "the act or result of"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: The act, or the faculty, of looking back on things past
vocabulary.context: Blank and dreary on retrospection I call them; they were not so to me then.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “retrospection”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again") + -tion (Latin -tio, "the act of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: (a) Electricity excited by the mutual action of certain liquids and metals
vocabulary.context: Perhaps a corpse would be reanimated; galvanism had given token of such things: perhaps the component parts of a creature might be manufactured, brought together, and endued with vital warmth.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “galvanism”: -ism (Greek -ismos, "practice, belief"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The act of striking or giving blows
vocabulary.context: One which would speak to the mysterious fears of our nature, and awaken thrilling horror—one to make the reader dread to look round, to curdle the blood, and quicken the beatings of the heart.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “beating”: be- (Old English be-, "thoroughly, about"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Perhaps a corpse would be reanimated; galvanism had given token of such things: perhaps the component parts of a creature might be manufactured, brought together, and endued with vital warmth.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “reanimate”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again") + anim (Latin anima, "breath, soul") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: To belong or pertain, whether by right, nature, appointment, or custom
vocabulary.context: In all matters of discovery and invention, even of those that appertain to the imagination, we are continually reminded of the story of Columbus and his egg.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “appertain”: ap- (Latin ad, "to") + tain (Latin tenere, "to hold"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: A bed or cot for a baby, oscillating on rockers or swinginng on pivots
vocabulary.context: The shape was lost beneath the shadow of the castle walls; but soon a gate swung back, a step was heard, the door of the chamber opened, and he advanced to the couch of the blooming youths, cradled in healthy sleep.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “cradle”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: He was forever inciting me to obtain literary reputation, which even on my own part I cared for then, though since I have become infinitely indifferent to it.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “incite”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: A body of seats on the floor of a music hall or theater nearest the orchestra
vocabulary.context: I see them still; the very room, the dark parquet, the closed shutters, with the moonlight struggling through, and the sense I had that the glassy lake and white high Alps were beyond.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “parquet”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

context.history: The 1816 'year without a summer' followed the eruption of Mount Tambora. Galvani's experiments making frog legs twitch with electricity fed public speculation about reanimation.

significance: The Introduction is one of the most famous origin stories in literature and frames the novel as both a dream and a deliberate artistic creation, mirroring Victor's own act of making.
discussionQuestions: Shelley calls her book her 'hideous progeny.' How does that phrase connect the author to Victor?
Where does point of view appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with the costs of unchecked ambition?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Introduction,” how does Shelley show the origin of the novel and the idea of creation? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the point of view you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Introduction develops the idea of the origin of the novel and the idea of creation. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of point of view and allusion shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses point of view in Introduction to complicate the reader's understanding of the origin of the novel and the idea of creation. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Introduction within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of the origin of the novel and the idea of creation responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Introduction as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of the origin of the novel and the idea of creation. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

satQuestions.passage: I busied myself to think of a story—a story to rival those which had excited us to this task. One which would speak to the mysterious fears of our nature, and awaken thrilling horror—one to make the reader dread to look round, to curdle the blood, and quicken the beatings of the heart. If I did not accomplish these things, my ghost story would be unworthy of its name. I thought and pondered—vainly. I felt that blank incapability of invention which is the greatest misery of authorship, when dull Nothing replies to our anxious invocations. Have you thought of a story? I was asked each morning, and each morning I was forced to reply with a mortifying negative.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Introduction”?
options: The origin of the novel and the idea of creation

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Shelley calls her book her 'hideous progeny.' How does that phrase connect the author to Victor? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are platitude, invocations, retrospection, galvanism, beatings. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “The illustrious poets also, annoyed by the platitude of prose, speedily relinquished their uncongenial task.” Webster's says: The quality or state of being flat, thin, or insipid. Now the word history: “platitude”: -ude (Latin -udo, "state of"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “invocation”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in") + voc (Latin vocare, "to call") + -ation (Latin -atio, "the act or result of"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “retrospection”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again") + -tion (Latin -tio, "the act of"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Frankenstein would have known. The 1816 'year without a summer' followed the eruption of Mount Tambora. Galvani's experiments making frog legs twitch with electricity fed public speculation about reanimation. Why does this chapter matter? The Introduction is one of the most famous origin stories in literature and frames the novel as both a dream and a deliberate artistic creation, mirroring Victor's own act of making. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for point of view.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see point of view, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to the origin of the novel and the idea of creation.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Point of view, Allusion, Imagery.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of point of view. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
